title: A time to die
hookLine: to every thing a season: a time to be born, and a time to die
last: ESTABLISH THOU THE WORK OF OUR HANDS.

cards: What season is it? Not on the calendar. In a life.
The book of Ecclesiastes has an answer, and it comes as a list. "To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven: A time to be born, and a time to die."
And the list goes on from there, pair after pair. Why does dying sit right near the top of it?

teach.b: First, the speaker. Ecclesiastes is spoken by someone the Hebrew calls Koheleth, rendered in English as the Teacher or the Preacher.
He has looked hard at everything done under the sun, and all of it, he says, is vanity, a word some readers hear as breath or vapor: real, and gone quickly. Second, the list.

teach.h: A LIST OF TIMES, IN PAIRS.
teach.b: Then he lays out the times of a life in pairs. Born and die. Plant and pluck up.
Break down and build up. "A time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance." A time to keep silence, and a time to speak.
Death isn't hidden at the end of the list or left off it. It's the second thing named, right beside being born. The list doesn't say which times are good and which are bad.
It says each one has its time, and a life holds them all. Fourth, beauty in its time.
A few verses later the Teacher writes, "He hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart." Some readers translate that word not as world but as eternity.
Either way, it names something odd about being human: we live inside one season, and still long to see the whole. The Teacher doesn't fix that. He leaves the list standing.
Some Jewish communities read the whole of Ecclesiastes at Sukkot, the harvest festival, a joyful time, listening to a book that never looks away from death.

how: Jews read Ecclesiastes as part of the Hebrew Bible, and some communities read the whole book at Sukkot; Christians read it too, and its list of times is sometimes read at funerals.

games.q: you're the Teacher, writing down the times of a human life. where do you put dying?
o: put it last, as the end of everything.
right at the start, paired with being born.
games.why: a time to be born, and a time to die: the very first pair. death isn't hidden. it has its season like everything else.

practice: Run the Teacher's list through your own life: planting or uprooting, breaking down or building up, weeping or laughing, mourning or dancing, keeping silence or speaking, each pair passing slowly with your breath.
When one catches, stay there; maybe it's two at once, and the list allows that. Name the season you're in, in a word or two, without judging whether it's a good one.

wordCard.voice: Koheleth, the Hebrew name for the Teacher who speaks Ecclesiastes and lists a season for everything, death named right beside birth. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: et, a time, the word that repeats down the list in Ecclesiastes 3.

carryVoice: Your line: a time for everything. Each season in its time, none left off the list. That's day seven hundred seventy-six.
